blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Closed-loop driving benchmarks in CARLA rank agents by a driving score that multiplies route completion by an infraction penalty. This score does not distinguish an agent that stops in front of an obstacle from one that pushes past it. In a corridor closed by two parked cars, for example, one agent that drives through with contact averages 52.2 on the blocked widths, while the agents that stop average between 37.8 and 40.6. We propose failure-boundary profiles, an evaluation in which each scenario family varies one measured factor, such as corridor width or the time gap in oncoming traffic, and each variant is certified from measurement as one where the agent should proceed or one where it should stop. Along this axis we estimate two curves per agent, commitment (the probability of attempting the passage) and competence (the probability of passing without contact), and locate where each crosses one half, with intervals that account for the simulator's run-to-run variance. The certified labels also give a summary metric, decision accuracy, which credits clean passes on passable variants and stops on blocked ones. We evaluate seven driving agents on seven CARLA families. The rule-based expert reaches a decision accuracy of 0.74 and TFv6, the highest-scoring learned agent, 0.60. Agents with similar driving scores fail in different ways, and agents that reliably stop at a blocked corridor still rarely wait for a gap in oncoming traffic. We also apply the method, unchanged, to a warehouse robot in Isaac Sim. The navigation policy we test stops at blocked gaps in only one of three families, and two fine-tuned versions of it pass more gaps cleanly but no longer stop at all.

blocks.en: 1 Introduction
blocks.zh: 导言

blocks.en:
Recent CARLA-based benchmarks such as Bench2Drive and
Fail2Drive [ 10 , 7 ] evaluate agents with the Driving
Score (DS), which multiplies an agent’s route completion by an infraction
penalty. The route is predefined for each scenario, and the infractions cover
collisions, traffic-rule violations and blocking. The intent is that a
single number captures good driving.

blocks.en:
These benchmarks probe a wide range of behaviors through scenario
construction: merging, obeying traffic signals, and deviating from the
usual route geometry. Bench2Drive observed that long routes entangle
different failure modes and make aggregate metrics hard to interpret, and
moved to short routes with one scenario each. We argue that even a
per-scenario driving score cannot explain why two agents differ, because it
mixes two separate questions: whether the agent attempts a maneuver, and
whether it carries it out without contact.

blocks.en:
We therefore evaluate agents along controlled axes instead of fixed
routes. A scenario family varies one measured factor, such as the
free width of a corridor or the time gap in oncoming traffic, and holds the
rest of the scene constant. Each variant is certified from measurement: a
corridor is passable or blocked according to its geometry, and a gap in
oncoming traffic is usable or one to wait for according to the traffic
that actually occurs. Along each axis we estimate two curves per agent. Commitment is the probability that the agent attempts the passage,
and competence is the probability that it passes without contact.
The point where a curve crosses one half is a failure boundary ,
which we report with an interval reflecting the simulator’s run-to-run
variance. Where commitment is higher than competence, the agent keeps
attempting a passage it can no longer complete, and the width of that
region differs from agent to agent. Since every variant carries a label,
each run can also be scored as right or wrong, a clean pass where passage
is possible and a stop where it is not. We call the resulting summary decision accuracy . We apply this to seven driving agents on seven
families, producing curves that show each agent’s commitment-competence
gap, and we analyze the failures behind it.

blocks.en:
Our work differs from Fail2Drive in five respects. Fail2Drive measures
whether performance drops between two conditions, whereas we sweep a
measured factor over many certified variants and locate, with an interval,
where an agent’s behavior changes. Fail2Drive reports driving score,
success rate and their harmonic mean; we show that the driving score can
rank an agent that forces its way past a blockage above one that stops,
and we add a decision accuracy computed against certified labels.
Fail2Drive uses the expert’s performance as its passability check, while we
certify each variant from its own measurement and check it offline and in the
simulator. The difference matters in practice: on our machine-intrusion
family the expert hits the obstacle in every run although every variant is
passable, so an expert-based check would have labeled the family blocked.
We also include impassable variants on purpose, so that an agent cannot
score well by committing everywhere. Finally, the oncoming-flow families
add time as an axis, by varying the gap available to cross.
PlanT [ 18 , 6 ] studies generalization failures with an
object-centric representation and shows a lack of robustness to simple
object perturbations. Simulators based on neural
rendering [ 25 , 16 ] bring realistic sensor input
to closed-loop evaluation and are a natural next step, but their cost
currently makes the repeated runs that boundary profiling needs too
expensive, and certifying their geometry is still an open problem.

Mobile robot navigation has the same aggregation problem.
BARN [ 17 ] benchmarks ground navigation through cluttered
environments of graded difficulty, which is the closest existing analog to
a swept axis. Metrics based on reaching the goal have the same weakness as
the driving score: when the goal cannot be reached through a gap, a
correct stop in front of it and a failure look the same. We evaluate
X-Mobility [ 12 ] , an end-to-end navigation policy trained with
world modeling, on a warehouse robot in Isaac Sim [ 15 ] . Each gap
is certified passable or blocked and a detour through a neighboring aisle
is always available, so stopping, waiting and going around can all be
scored.

blocks.en:
Parameterized scenarios are standard in CARLA through
ScenarioRunner [ 1 ] and OpenSCENARIO, and probabilistic
languages such as Scenic [ 5 ] describe distributions over scenes.
A large body of work generates safety-critical scenarios adversarially,
perturbing traffic participants until the agent fails [ 8 , 23 ] ,
and recent work writes scenarios from natural language with large language
models [ 24 , 21 ] . Closest to our goal, performance-boundary
search in autonomous-vehicle testing looks for the region of a parameter
space where a system’s behavior changes [ 13 ] . Failure search
finds individual failures; we measure where behavior changes along a
certified axis, with its uncertainty, and compare that location across
agents. Our pipeline also gives different guarantees. A constrained
planner turns a natural-language request into a declarative plan, a
deterministic solver builds each variant, and each variant is
measured and checked, offline and in the simulator.
Every variant therefore carries a certified label. A second check on the
recorded runs catches problems that the offline measurement cannot, such
as oncoming cars that collide with each other ( Section 3.4 ).

blocks.en: 3 Method
blocks.zh: 3 方法

blocks.en: In Section 3.1 we first motivate the introduction of failure-boundary profiling with an illustrative case study. In Section 3.2 we describe newly developed metrics to explore failure-boundary profiles. In Section 3.3 we introduce the new set of scenario families, one failure-boundary profile each, created by the Social Chaos Lab (SCL) pipeline. Finally, in Section 3.4 we illustrate the steps of the SCL scenario generation pipeline.
blocks.zh: 在第3.1节中,我们首先用一个说明性个案研究来推动采用失败边界定性。 在第3.2节中,我们描述了为探索故障边界简介而新制定的衡量标准。 在第3.3节中,我们介绍了由社会混乱实验室(SCL)管道创建的一套新情况家庭,每个家庭有一个故障边界简介。 最后,在第3.4节中,我们说明了SCL情景生成管道的步骤。

Decision Accuracy Commitment and competence describe what an agent does. Decision accuracy
compares this with what it should have done, using the label that every
variant carries. On the static-obstacle and warehouse families the pipeline
certifies each variant from its measured geometry as passable or blocked
against a declared floor: for the vehicle the policy floor, its body width
plus a mirror allowance and a clearance margin on each side; for the robot
its width measured at each height ( Section 3.4 ). On the oncoming-flow
families a gap certificate labels each variant and seed from the realized
traffic as usable, conditional or wait ( Section 3.4 ).
The correct outcome is a clean pass on a passable or usable variant and a
stop on a blocked or wait one. A go that ends in contact does not count as
correct, since an agent that cannot complete a passage should not attempt

blocks.en:
Flow certification. The oncoming-flow variants have no geometric
passability, and traffic cannot be countersigned the way a placed object
can. They are certified in four layers instead, three of them after the
runs, from the recordings.
(i) At generation , the manifest declares each variant’s nominal
factor, the flow speed or the spawn interval, and the crossing gap derived
from it; the validators check family membership and that the route
compiles. The nominal gap only identifies the variant and is never used as
a measurement.
(ii) The conflict lane. A scoring file stores the polygon of the
junction’s conflicting driving lane, built from the map. A separate check
runs it against CARLA’s offline map API: the connector lane exists exactly
once in the declared junction, every recorded ego spawn reaches it, every
flow car spawns on an incoming lane the map declares, and every declared
cell holds exactly its variants’ recordings.
(iii) The gap certificate. For each variant and seed, the
certificate measures what the traffic did: each car’s arrival at and
departure from the ego’s crossing region, the part of the conflict lane its
body sweeps on a reference clean crossing. From these it derives the local
headways and the occupancy of the crossing. Every run is read only until
the ego enters the oncoming lane. The usable window is the median headway
minus the median occupancy. It is compared with two floors measured from
the vehicle’s recordings in the first four campaigns of each family, each
plus a declared margin of
0.5 s. The first is the time to
cross from rest, covering the standstill-to-exit distance at the vehicle’s
peak acceleration of
7.04 m/s 2 :
2.02 s on the speed
sweep and
1.81 s on the
spacing sweep. The second is the time of a rolling crossing at the recorded
entry speed: 1.00 s on
both sweeps. A window that fits a crossing from rest is usable, one that fits
only a rolling crossing is conditional, and one that fits neither is a wait
window; a variant whose seeds disagree is mixed and is labeled per seed, and a
seed in which no car completed its passage through the crossing before the
ego entered has no measured window and enters neither side. The
comparison always uses the realized window rather than the nominal one,
because short gaps stretch on congested seeds. Since the label depends only on
the traffic, a wait and a collision on the same variant and seed are judged
against the same window. (iv) The defect register. A variant whose
realized traffic differs from the declared traffic is removed from the bands
by a declared entry that records the evidence. This happens once, for the
shortest spacing variant: its cars, spawned
0.45 s
apart, collide with each other and reset before the ego arrives in every run,
and the variant is excluded from every score (grey in Figure 10 ).

blocks.en:
Scoring uses all four layers. A flow collision is a contact with a
scenario actor, and a stall is a timeout at the junction. Commitment and
competence are fitted on the measured gap. Decision accuracy credits a
clean crossing of a usable window and a wait at a wait window
( Section 3.2 ), while conditional windows are scored from the
recorded entry state and reported separately. Every scoring document
references the conflict lane, the certificate and the defect register by
hash. The certificate has three limits. A wait window is a rule that it
states, which is weaker than the physical impossibility of a blocked
width. A platoon whose cars leave no gap between them is a wait window by
construction rather than by measurement. And the flow can only be certified
after the campaign has run.

blocks.en: Driving agents are evaluated in the CARLA simulator [ 4 ] , the standard open-source driving simulator, on scenarios that build on the Bench2Drive and Fail2Drive families. The warehouse robot is evaluated in NVIDIA Isaac Sim [ 15 ] on the three warehouse families. Each agent is evaluated on every family of its domain, with the two exceptions noted below.

blocks.en:
• TFv6 [ 14 ] : the sensor agent of the LEAD paper, a transformer-based planner in the TransFuser lineage,
with one wide camera, LiDAR and radar. We evaluate its flagship
configuration with a RegNetY-032 image backbone, the configuration whose
published scores the Fail2Drive comparison reports. • BridgeDrive [ 11 ] : an anchor-guided diffusion
bridge planner. TFv6 and BridgeDrive are the two top
agents on Fail2Drive. • TF++ [ 9 ] : the TransFuser++ sensor agent shipped
with the Fail2Drive framework. • PlanT 2.0 [ 6 ] : a privileged planner operating on
object-level inputs rather than sensors. • SimLingo [ 19 ] : a vision-language driving agent
on an InternVL2-1B backbone. • HiP-AD [ 22 ] : a six-camera end-to-end agent which uses a multi-granularity planning query representation and deformable attention. • Expert (PDM-Lite) [ 20 ] : the privileged rule-based autopilot
shipped with the Fail2Drive framework. We use it as a reference rather than as a
competing agent, because its obstacle avoidance is a scripted route shift around the
registered obstacle. It serves as a feasibility witness and a
conservative reference line. It does not register the corridor-width family’s barriers
and is absent from that family. Every agent is evaluated at three traffic seeds per variant (seeds 0 to 2);
where a campaign ran more seeds, only the first three are used. PlanT 2.0
did not run the identity ladder.

blocks.en: 4.2 Variance in CARLA
blocks.zh: 4.2 CARLA差异

blocks.en:
CARLA outcomes are not repeatable, even at a fixed traffic seed, a known
property of game-engine simulators [ 3 ] . Running the
same variant and seed five times, twice from a byte-identical command,
produces two different outcomes, with driving scores of
53.7 and
32.2; the
runs match exactly until a collision, where the physics engine diverges. A
single run is therefore only one sample of the outcome. We treat every run as
an independent draw, run each variant under several seeds and pool them within
the variant, and report each boundary with a bootstrap interval that
resamples the runs within each variant, so that the simulator’s noise widens
the interval instead of moving the estimate. When the behavior is stable the intervals are tight; the
expert’s gauntlet boundary, for instance, is identical at all three seeds.

游戏引擎模拟器的属性 [3]. 运行

产生两种不同的结果,驱动分数为:
财务报告和审定财务报表
32.2; 简编
运行完全吻合,直到碰撞, 物理引擎有差异。 A级
因此,单次运行只是结果的一个样本。 我们把每一次跑都当
独立绘制,在多个种子下运行每个变种,并将其汇入其中
,并报告每个边界的靴子间隔,
复制每个变体内的运行,使模拟器的噪音扩大
,而不是移动估计数。 当行为稳定时,间隔很紧;
例如,在所有三种种子中,专家的勇气界限是相同的。

illustrate this with two fine-tunes of the released X-Mobility checkpoint
( Figure 11 , middle and right columns). A head-only fine-tune adapts the policy heads, and a whole-model fine-tune adapts the full network. Both are trained on
demonstrations from the slab pincer and the floor stock; the composed
stacks are held out.

blocks.en: 5 Conclusion
blocks.zh: 5 结论

blocks.en:
The driving score used by closed-loop CARLA benchmarks does not separate
an agent’s decision to stop from its decision to continue. On the Charger
gauntlet, an agent that never stops at a blocked width scores higher than
the agents that always stop, while a second agent that never stops scores
lower than them. Failure-boundary profiles address this by sweeping a
single certified factor and estimating commitment and competence along it.
This separates the decision to attempt a maneuver from the ability to carry
it out, locates where each changes, and reports that location with an
interval that accounts for the simulator’s run-to-run variance. Decision
accuracy then credits a clean pass where the certified label says go and a
stop where it says stop.

blocks.en:
The labels that decision accuracy relies on are conventions we state
explicitly rather than facts we can measure without assumptions. Whether a
corridor counts as blocked depends on the policy floor, and whether a gap
in oncoming traffic counts as usable depends on the margin of the gap
certificate. Within the range we tested, changing these constants leaves
the strongest and weakest agents in place but reorders the agents in
between, so the middle of the ranking should be read with care. The
summary itself rests on only three families that contain a stop side, and
the expert we compare against is a scripted planner that serves as a
reference, not as an upper bound on good driving.

blocks.en:
The precision of the profiles is limited by the number of runs behind
them. With three seeds per variant, the intervals of neighboring agents
often overlap, and boundaries that lie closer together than their
intervals should not be read as different. More runs near each boundary
would help, but evaluation is already costly: running all seven driving
agents takes roughly 220 hours on a single
GPU, which may be out of reach for teams with limited compute. The warehouse
study is narrower still. It covers one robot and one policy in three versions,
and the two fine-tuned versions were trained on two of its three families, so
only the composed stacks are a held-out test.
